title: The Tell-Tale Heart after
author: Salon
note: He can tell it calmly. The pulse under the Queens floorboards will not stay calm. After Poe, The Tell-Tale Heart, 1843.

scenes.title: The walk-up
scenes.reentry: Listen. I can tell this calmly.

breaths.text: Listen. I can tell this calmly.
That is how you will know I am not mad.
Madness is disorder, and what I did was orderly—measured, patient, almost tender.
I have never been more precise.
I lived with the old man in a third-floor walk-up off Roosevelt.
He had been there first; I took the smaller room when the rent became impossible alone.
He was kind in the soft, irritating way of people who forgive you too quickly.
He left tea bags on the counter for me.
He asked about my shifts at the hospital cafeteria.
None of that mattered.
What mattered was the eye.
One eye was filmed over, pale as milk left too long.
When he looked at me with it, something in my chest tightened until I could taste metal.
I loved him.
I want that clear.
I loved him and I could not bear the eye.
At breakfast it rested on my hands.
At night, if his door stood ajar, it found me in the hall like a pale coin.
For a week I practiced.
Every night near midnight I opened his door by degrees—hinge oiled with cooking grease, breath held—until I could slide my head into the dark and wait.
The building made its usual sounds: a neighbor's television through the plaster, the elevator complaining two floors down, a phone vibrating somewhere and going unanswered.
Once a scooter shrieked on the street and I nearly laughed aloud at my own stillness.
I held a stripped flashlight closed in my fist and opened it only when I was sure.
Seven nights the eye was shut.
Seven nights I withdrew like someone closing a curtain.
On the eighth night my thumb slipped on the switch.
A thin click.
The old man sat up.
"Who's there?" he said.
I did not answer.
I stood in the doorway for an hour while he listened to the dark the way I had listened to him.
Fear has a sound; I knew it in my own throat on bad nights after work.
When at last I opened the light to a thread, it fell exactly on the filmed eye—wide, wet, unbearable.
The rest of his face stayed in shadow, as if the eye alone had insisted on being seen.
Afterward, under the mattress, the heart kept going for a while, muffled, like a watch wrapped in a sock.
Then it stopped.
I worked with the care of someone cleaning before guests: plastic sheeting from the dollar store, the tub, the loose floorboards under the rug I had always hated.
By morning the room smelled of bleach and cold coffee.
No stain.
No proof.
Only the quiet of a radiator ticking and my own hands, very steady, washing themselves raw.
The officers came because a neighbor had heard a cry.
I smiled.
I showed them the kitchen, the fire escape, his empty bed made neatly.
I said he was visiting a sister in Jersey.
I offered them chairs in his room and sat myself on the rug, directly above what I had hidden, because confidence is a kind of camouflage.
They believed me.
Of course they did.
I spoke steadily.
I even laughed once, lightly, at a joke about the neighborhood traffic.
One of them checked his phone and put it away.
The other accepted water.
Then the sound began.
At first I thought it was the pipes.
Then a phone left face-down somewhere under a cushion.
Then I understood: soft, quick, cotton-wrapped, rising through the boards into the bones of my feet.
I talked faster.
I scraped my chair.
I offered more water, a pastry I did not have.
The officers kept chatting, polite, unhurried, while the beat climbed into my skull and made a mockery of every careful thing I had done.
I could see their mouths moving.
I could not hear their words over it.
Louder. Louder.
The eye was gone and still the heart would not shut up.
Sweat ran into my collar.
The fluorescent fixture in the hall buzzed like an insect trapped in glass.
I stood.
The chair fell.
Something in my voice broke open, raw and ridiculous.
"Stop smiling," I shouted.
"You hear it—you hear it—tear up the floor—here—here—it is his heart—"
